nameStory: The northern cardita gets its name from its heart-shaped outline when viewed from the side, with 'cardita' meaning 'little heart' in Latin. The 'northern' part of its name reflects its preference for the cooler waters of the North Atlantic, where it thrives in chilly conditions that would be too harsh for many other shellfish.
description: The northern cardita is a small, chunky clam with a distinctive heart-shaped profile that makes it stand out among New England's coastal shells. This hardy bivalve typically measures about an inch across and has thick, sturdy shells with prominent ridges radiating from the hinge area. Unlike the smooth, streamlined shells of many beach clams, carditas have a robust, almost armored appearance that reflects their ability to survive in harsh northern waters. You'll find their empty shells washed up on beaches, often still connected at the hinge.

idTips.label: Heart-shaped profile
idTips.description: When viewed from the side, the shell has a distinctive heart or triangular outline that's much more angular than typical rounded clams

idTips.label: Radiating ridges
idTips.description: Strong, raised ridges fan out from the hinge area like spokes on a wheel, creating deep grooves you can feel with your finger

idTips.label: Thick, heavy shell
idTips.description: The shell feels surprisingly heavy and solid for its size, much thicker than a typical beach clam of similar dimensions

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: Rarely grows larger than an inch across, fitting comfortably in the palm of a child's hand

idTips.label: Whitish to gray color
idTips.description: Fresh shells are often chalky white to pale gray, sometimes with brownish staining from sediment

habitat: Northern carditas live in cold ocean waters along New England's rocky coasts and muddy sea floors, typically in deeper waters offshore. Their empty shells wash up on sandy and rocky beaches throughout the region, especially after winter storms. You're most likely to find them while beachcombing on Maine's coast and other northern New England shores where cold Atlantic currents dominate.

seasonality.spring: Fresh shells begin washing ashore as spring storms stir up the sea floor. This is when you'll find the whitest, least weathered specimens.
seasonality.summer: Beach-worn shells are common finds during summer beachcombing, though they may be bleached and smoothed by sun and surf.
seasonality.fall: Fall storms bring new shells to shore, often still paired together at the hinge before winter weather separates them.
seasonality.winter: Winter storms deposit the most shells on beaches, but harsh conditions make beachcombing challenging except on calmer days.

funFact: Northern carditas are living time capsules that can survive for decades in the frigid Arctic Ocean, with some specimens found to be over 30 years old despite being smaller than a ping pong ball!
confusionNotes: The northern cardita's heart-shaped profile and radiating ridges make it hard to confuse with other New England shells, but beginners might mistake weathered specimens for small scallops. Remember: carditas have ridges that radiate from one point (the hinge), while scallops have ridges that fan out from the entire hinge line like a hand fan.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'false-cockle' in its family name, the northern cardita isn't trying to fool anyone - it's just that early shell collectors thought it looked similar to true cockles before understanding the anatomical differences between the two families.
compareHints: The northern cardita is the only member of its genus found in New England waters, making it unique in the region. Compared to other members of the false-cockle family found elsewhere, it's distinguished by its particularly pronounced heart shape and its adaptation to extremely cold northern waters. Its closest relatives in warmer waters tend to be larger and less angular in profile.
